Every 20-year stretch since 1914: how much a dollar lost, and how wide the range has been

A single inflation assumption hides how differently decades have turned out. Using Statistics Canada’s CPI back to 1914, see what a dollar kept over every overlapping 10, 20 or 30-year window, how often prices rose faster than a planning assumption, and how often a steady return after fees and tax kept up.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Every stretch of years since 1914: how much a dollar lost, and how wide the range was

Across 92 overlapping 20-year windows of Canadian CPI, the median rise in prices was 2.82% a year. The fastest was 1971–1991 at 7.13% a year, when a dollar kept 25 cents of its buying power, so $50,000 of today’s spending would need $198,164; at your 2.5% assumption it needs $81,931. 55% of windows ran hotter than your assumption. A steady 4.00% a year after fees and tax would have kept purchasing power in 75% of them. History is a range of past outcomes, not a forecast.

The central idea

Across the 92 overlapping 20-year windows from 1914–1934 to 2005–2025, Canadian prices rose by a median of 2.82% a year, but the range ran from prices falling 1.75% a year (1920–1940) to rising 7.13% a year (1971–1991), when a dollar kept only about a quarter of its buying power. A goal costing CAD 50,000 today needs about CAD 81,900 in 20 years at 2.5% inflation, and about CAD 198,200 if prices rose as they did over 1971–1991. A steady 4% a year after fees and tax kept purchasing power in 75% of the 20-year windows and 62% of the 30-year windows. History shows the spread a plan should allow for; it does not say which part of it comes next.

01

One number for inflation, many possible decades

A long-term plan usually needs one inflation figure: 2% or 2.5% a year is common, and the Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range. That target is a policy aim, and the Bank says it was adopted with the Government of Canada only in 1991. A saver who is 35 today is planning across 30 years or more, and over a span that long the average result has varied far more than the year-to-year noise suggests.

This guide uses Statistics Canada’s Consumer Price Index from January 1914 to look at every overlapping stretch of years: 1914 to 1934, 1915 to 1935, and so on up to 2005 to 2025. For each one it asks how much a dollar could still buy at the end. The inflation basics guide explains how a constant rate compounds; this one shows how far real decades have strayed from any constant rate.

02

A century of yearly inflation, and why the averages need care

The first chart compares each calendar year’s average CPI with the year before. Prices rose 17.96% in 1917 and fell 12.11% in 1921; they fell in ten years in all, the last in 1953. Every year from 1973 to 1982 was above 7%. More recently, inflation was 6.80% in 2022 and 2.07% in 2025, and the index for September 2026 was 3.09% above September 2025.

These are dated observations, with two cautions. The basket and the methods behind the CPI have changed many times since 1914, so the early figures describe a different set of purchases from today’s. And an annual average smooths the months: a year-over-year change in a single month, the figure usually quoted in the news, can differ from the change in the annual average. The CPI measurement guide covers those differences.

03

What a dollar kept over every 20-year window

The second chart divides the average index in the first year of each window by the average in its last year. With 20-year windows, the median result was inflation of 2.82% a year, close to many planning assumptions. But the worst window, 1971 to 1991, averaged 7.13% a year: CAD 1 at the start could buy only what CAD 0.25 had bought. In the best, 1920 to 1940, prices fell 1.75% a year and a dollar bought more at the end than at the start. Seven of the 92 windows ended with prices lower than they began, and all of them started between 1917 and 1923.

Change the window length to see how the spread narrows and widens. Over 10 years the median is 2.35% a year, but the worst window, 1972 to 1982, averaged 9.60%. Over 30 years the median is 3.07% and the worst, 1963 to 1993, averaged 5.72%, enough to cut a dollar to about 19 cents. Longer windows average out good and bad years, yet the total difference between them still grows, because it compounds for longer. The windows overlap, so neighbouring points share most of their years; there are only a handful of truly separate 20 or 30-year periods in the record.

04

How often history ran hotter than your assumption

The third chart counts the windows by their average inflation. With the default 2.5% assumption, 55% of the 20-year windows ran above it. That does not mean a 55% chance of the next 20 years doing so: the record includes two world wars, the Depression and the oil shocks, and the inflation-targeting era since the 1990s has been calmer. Set the first year to 1991 and the windows reflect only that era, which leaves far fewer of them to judge by.

The practical use is a stress test. A goal costing CAD 50,000 in today’s dollars needs about CAD 81,900 in 20 years at 2.5% a year, about CAD 87,200 at the 2.82% median and about CAD 198,200 if prices rose as they did from 1971 to 1991. A plan does not have to be built on the worst window, but it helps to know what a higher path would require: more saving, a later date, a smaller goal or a mix with more growth potential and more risk. The price-level guide shows why prices do not fall back after a burst of inflation slows.

05

What return kept up, before and after fees and tax

The heatmap takes a steady yearly return, removes the fee you enter, taxes what is left at the rate you enter, and counts the share of past windows in which it at least matched the rise in prices. A steady 4% with no fee or tax kept purchasing power in 75% of the 20-year windows and 62% of the 30-year windows; 6% kept up in every 30 and 40-year window. A 1.5% fee turns that 4% into 2.5%, which kept up over 20 years in fewer than half of the windows.

Tax matters in the same way. Interest earned outside a registered account is taxed every year on its full nominal amount, including the part that only replaces lost buying power; at a 40% rate, 4% interest leaves 2.4%. CRA says that interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn, so the account can matter as much as the investment. The tax treatment comes from the account, not from the fund itself: the same balanced fund is taxed differently in a TFSA, an RRSP and a non-registered account, as the guide to tax on inflation gains shows.

06

Why a balanced fund is not the steady line in the grid

The grid uses constant returns because they make the comparison exact, not because any investment delivers one. A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds, and its return varies widely from year to year, with losses in some years. High-inflation periods were often hard on both parts at once: rising interest rates push bond prices down, and the guide to years when stocks and bonds fall together uses 2022 as an example. Equities have historically offered more growth potential over long periods than cash, but with larger declines, and no return or recovery by a particular date is assured.

What the history does support is that money expected to be spent decades from now has to be judged in real terms. Cash and short-term deposits protect the nominal amount, which matters for money needed soon, but over long windows they have often lost purchasing power after tax. Holding a growth-oriented share of a long-term plan is one response to that, with risk that has to suit the person and the time available; the balanced-fund crash and inflation guide sets those risks side by side.

07

Saving from pay through a high-inflation decade

For someone saving from each paycheque, inflation acts on both sides of the plan. A fixed monthly contribution shrinks in real terms if it is never raised, while pay has, over long periods, tended to rise with prices, though not in every year or for every worker. Raising contributions once a year by the CPI keeps the real amount saved roughly level; the indexed contributions guide shows the difference over a career. That is a different situation from a lump sum already saved, where the question is how the existing balance is invested and in which account, not how much new money to add.

08

What this history can and cannot tell you

  • Windows overlap, so the counts are not independent observations; the record holds only a few separate 30-year periods.
  • The CPI is an average basket. Your own costs, such as rent, food or care, can rise faster or slower; the personal inflation guide shows how to weigh them.
  • Annual averages are used throughout. A window measured from one month to another gives slightly different results.
  • The returns in the grid are constant by construction, with the fee and tax applied every year. Real returns vary, taxes depend on the account and the type of income, and fees change.
  • None of this forecasts inflation, interest rates or investment returns, and none of it is a recommendation to buy or sell any investment.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first three charts use the all-items Consumer Price Index for Canada (Statistics Canada table 18-10-0004-01, vector v41690973, 2002=100), retrieved through Statistics Canada’s Web Data Service on 27 October 2026 with monthly values from January 1914 to September 2026. Calendar-year averages of the twelve monthly values for 1914 to 2025 are compared with each other; 2026 is incomplete and is used only for the latest 12-month change. The fourth chart applies hypothetical constant returns to those same windows. Nothing here is a forecast of inflation or of any investment’s return. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

    All-items CPI for Canada, 2002=100, vector v41690973. Reviewed 27 October 2026. Source of every inflation figure in the first three charts and the text.

  2. Statistics Canada · Web Data Service, getDataFromVectorsAndLatestNPeriods for vector 41690973 ↗

    Retrieved 27 October 2026 (POST request for the latest 1,500 periods): 1,353 monthly values from January 1914 (6.0) to September 2026 (170.0), with twelve values in every year from 1914 to 2025. Annual averages are the mean of each year’s twelve values. SHA-256 of the retrieved file dd3e814c0c074771985921c902b5a23165f63e44757f9b7b9ce64fd1c148b440, kept locally and not republished.

  3. Statistics Canada · The Daily, Consumer Price Index, September 2026 ↗

    Release of 19 October 2026, the most recent monthly CPI at the time of review; the series value for September 2026 used here (170.0) was released that day and is 3.09% above September 2025 (164.9).

  4. Bank of Canada · Inflation-control target ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range, adopted in 1991 and most recently renewed in December 2021 for the five years to the end of 2026. Mentioned for context only; no figure from it is used in the charts.

  5. Canada Revenue Agency · What is a TFSA ↗

    Page dated 17 September 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026 for interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA generally being tax-free, even when withdrawn.
